tool_args.old_string:
Episodes within the same task type share environment dynamics, raising the concern that the effective sample size is closer to $K$ (task types) than $N$ (episodes). We address this with cluster-robust inference treating each task type as a cluster ($K{=}7$ clusters with non-empty data).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & $p$-value & 95\% CI \\
\midrule
Cluster-robust $t$-test (df$=$6) & $0.0001$ & $[0.213, 0.380]$ \\
Wild cluster bootstrap ($B{=}9{,}999$) & $0.014$ & $[0.239, 0.361]$ \\
Exact permutation (128 perms) & $0.016$ & --- \\
Sign test & $0.016$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Cluster-level tests of death-rate asymmetry ($K{=}7$ task clusters). All 7 clusters show internal DR $>$ deterministic DR (100\% directional consistency). Cohen's $d = 3.27$. The permutation $p = 0.016$ is the theoretical minimum for two-sided $K{=}7$ ($2/2^7 = 1/64$).}
\label{tab:wild-cluster}
\end{table}

\noindent All methods confirm significance, with CIs excluding zero by a wide margin. The wild cluster bootstrap and exact permutation $p$-values ($0.014$ and $0.016$) are conservative relative to the cluster-robust $t$-test ($0.0001$), as expected with few clusters.
tool_args.new_string:
Episodes within the same task type share environment dynamics, raising the concern that the effective sample size is closer to $K$ (task types) than $N$ (episodes). We address this with cluster-robust inference treating each task type as a cluster ($K{=}11$, all 11 included task types, 245 episodes).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & $p$-value & 95\% CI \\
\midrule
Cluster-robust $t$-test ($t{=}10.0$, df$=$10) & $< 0.001$ & $[0.73, 1.00]$ \\
Wild cluster bootstrap ($B{=}9{,}999$) & $< 0.001$ & $[0.73, 1.00]$ \\
Exact permutation ($2{,}048$ perms) & $0.002$ & --- \\
Sign test & $< 0.001$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Cluster-level tests of death-rate asymmetry ($K{=}11$ task clusters, 245 episodes). 10 of 11 clusters show internal DR $>$ deterministic DR; the sole exception (\texttt{find-non-living-thing}) has zero deaths under both strategies. Cohen's $d = 3.02$. The exact permutation $p = 0.002$ ($4/2{,}048$) reflects the near-unanimous directional consistency.}
\label{tab:wild-cluster}
\end{table}

\noindent All methods confirm significance with $p < 0.01$, and the 95\% CI $[0.73, 1.00]$ excludes zero by a wide margin. The $K{=}11$ analysis uses the same clusters as the main analysis, providing a direct robustness check on the primary results.

The framework requires only paired episode outcomes under two modalities with binary catastrophic indicators (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}, \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

The oracle router degenerates to unconditional deterministic computation (96.3\% decision overlap). Retry, $10{\times}$ model scaling, and Reflexion each fail to close the ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic execution. A failure mode taxonomy identifies the root mechanism: 100\% of internal-strategy deaths stem from a single action-space grounding failure (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}, Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}).

tool_args.old_string: All 73 internal-strategy deaths trace to a single action pattern: \texttt{focus on [object]}. In ScienceWorld, \texttt{focus on} is the answer-submission action; the LLM systematically misuses it as a general interaction command, applying it to irrelevant targets (rooms, doors, inventory items) and thereby submitting incorrect answers that trigger the $-100$ penalty. A taxonomy of death episodes (Appendix~\ref{app:failure-modes}) reveals that 69.9\% involve agents that correctly parse the task description but cannot ground their understanding in valid action primitives (Category B: comprehension without grounding). Only 21.9\% show no task awareness (Category A). The root cause is thus action-space grounding failure, not comprehension failure: 78.1\% of dying agents demonstrate task understanding, yet 97.3\% fail to translate it into correct actions. The deterministic strategy rarely executes \texttt{focus on} (${\sim}0.5\%$ of actions vs.\ $5.5\%$ for internal in death episodes), achieving 91.8\% survival (Figure~\ref{fig:death-comparison}). Among fatal targets, \texttt{workshop} alone accounts for 44.6\%, indicating a systematic object bias rather than random exploration (Figure~\ref{fig:death-action-dist}). This specificity suggests that targeted interventions (action-space filtering, grounding-aware prompting) could reduce death rates more effectively than general capability scaling.

The root cause is thus action-space grounding failure, not comprehension failure: 78.1\% of dying agents demonstrate task understanding, yet 97.3\% fail to translate it into correct actions.
